# Cautions

Things that could make a correct-looking analysis wrong. Read before
interpreting results.

- **Two odds ratios, two questions.** A random-intercept model gives an
  odds ratio for a given patient; a GEE gives one for the population. With
  large between-patient variation they can differ a lot. Neither is wrong;
  report the one that matches the question and say which it is.
- **Dichotomizing a pain score discards information.** "Any pain" matches
  the client's stated outcome, but an ordinal model of the full score is a
  reasonable secondary analysis.
- **"Cleaned" data is a claim, not a guarantee.** The source says the data
  have no problems; the pipeline still validates every range and code.
- **Odds ratios are non-collapsible.** Adjusting for a prognostic covariate
  moves an odds ratio away from one even with perfect balance, because the
  adjusted model answers a conditional question. A shift after adjustment is
  not evidence of confounding.
- **A common odds ratio is an assumption.** The single GEE odds ratio
  assumes the effect is the same at every assessment; the time-specific
  model checks it.
- **Covariate imbalance after randomization is chance.** Do not choose
  adjustment covariates by looking at Table 1.
- **One trial, one site.** Results describe this population of thoracic
  surgery patients with double-lumen tubes.
